I do use LLMs to build (like many engineers nowadays), but I also make sure changes are minimal, follow project culture, and well tested. I rebuilt Godot with the fix and tested it thoroughly.  Just thought I'd let you know -- at unity-mcp, we get a ton of slop too, so anyway, hello from a real human!

### Tested versions

Reproducible on 4.6.2-stable (official, macOS arm64). Not tested on other platforms but the code path is platform-independent.

### System information

macOS 26.3.1, Apple M1 Max, Godot 4.6.2-stable (official)

### Issue description

Any `@tool` editor plugin that calls `EditorInterface.save_scene()` from `_process()` crashes the editor instantly with a stack overflow (SIGSEGV). The editor becomes completely unusable — it crashes on startup as soon as the plugin is enabled and a scene is open.

**What happens:** `_save_scene_with_preview()` calls `EditorProgress::step()`, which calls `ProgressDialog::_update_ui()` → `Main::iteration()`. This runs a full frame cycle including `NOTIFICATION_PROCESS` on all `@tool` nodes. If any plugin's `_process()` triggers another save, the call chain re-enters `_save_scene_with_preview()` → `_update_ui()` → `Main::iteration()` → `_process()` recursively with no guard. The stack overflows after ~1000 frames.

This is the same class of bug as #54864, which was fixed for `EditorFileSystem` in #73214 using a `prevent_recursive_process_hack` static bool guard. That PR's description explicitly notes `Main::iteration()` inside `ProgressDialog` as "the ill nature of EditorProgress" and that it "will have to be entirely rewritten."

In the wild, this affects any plugin that does non-trivial `_process()` work (WebSocket polling, HTTP requests, file I/O) that can indirectly trigger a save. The MRP below simplifies the repro by calling `save_scene()` directly from `_process()`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a new project
2. Create a plugin with the MRP script below
3. Enable the plugin in Project Settings > Plugins
4. Open any scene
5. Editor crashes within seconds

```ini
name="Reentrant _process() Crash Repro"
description="MRP: triggers re-entrant _process() via Main::iteration() in ProgressDialog during save"
author="dsarno"
version="1.0"
script="plugin.gd"
```

```gdscript
@tool
extends EditorPlugin

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if EditorInterface.get_edited_scene_root():

```

Fixes #118544

**Note to maintainers:** This is not an AI slop PR..  I'm the lead maintainer on the 8,000 star Unity-MCP project. I do use LLMs to build (like many engineers), but I also make sure changes are minimal, follow project culture, and are well tested. I rebuilt Godot with the fix and tested it thoroughly. Just thought I'd let you know.  At unity-mcp, we get a ton of slop too, so anyway, hello from a real human!

## What happens

`ProgressDialog::_update_ui()` calls `Main::iteration()` with no re-entrancy guard. This runs a full frame cycle including `_process()` on all `@tool` nodes. If any plugin's `_process()` triggers a save (directly or indirectly), the call chain recurses: `_save_scene_with_preview` → `EditorProgress::step()` → `_update_ui()` → `Main::iteration()` → `_process()` → `save_scene()` → ... The stack overflows after ~1000 frames and the editor crashes (SIGSEGV).

## Fix

Adds a static `is_iterating` guard to `_update_ui()` — if `Main::iteration()` is already running from a prior `_update_ui()` call up the stack, the nested call is skipped. Same pattern as `prevent_recursive_process_hack` in `EditorFileSystem` (#73214 / #54864).

## Test plan

- [ ] Enable the MRP plugin from #118544 (a `@tool` plugin that calls `EditorInterface.save_scene()` from `_process()`)
- [ ] Without fix: editor crashes within seconds (SIGSEGV, stack overflow from 1000+ recursive `_process()` frames)
- [ ] With fix: editor stays alive, no recursion — `_update_ui()` returns early on re-entrant calls

- **Contribution gate:** Contributors are asked to consent to the repository AI rules before being allowed to use an AI on it.
- **AI workflow:** The AI is made aware of our contribution rules, such as the need to benchmark optimization changes, and helps enforce the rules by e.g. asking the user to test optimizations.

cases.body:
Add Multi-Scatter Energy Compensation to Improve Rough Specular Response

Summary

This PR introduces a multi-scatter energy compensation term in
shaders/scene_forward_clustered.glsl to improve the visual accuracy of specular reflections, particularly on rough metallic surfaces.

The change compensates for energy loss inherent in the current single-scatter GGX BRDF approximation, bringing Godot’s rendering closer to modern physically-based shading models used in other engines.

Motivation

Godot’s current specular model uses a single-scatter GGX approximation, which:

  • Underestimates reflected energy at higher roughness

  • Causes metals to appear darker and less saturated

  • Produces a “flat” or less rich appearance compared to other engines

This effect is further amplified when using tone mapping (e.g. AgX), resulting in noticeable loss of visual fidelity.

What this PR does

Adds a lightweight energy compensation factor after the BRDF LUT evaluation to approximate multi-scattering:

vec2 brdf = texture(brdf_lut, vec2(NdotV, roughness)).rg;
vec3 energy_compensation = 1.0 + F0 * (1.0 / brdf.y - 1.0);
specular *= energy_compensation;

Results

Visual improvements:

  • Rough metals appear brighter and more saturated

  • Improved energy conservation at high roughness values

  • More realistic response for:

    • metals (gold, steel, aluminum)

    • wet surfaces

    • coated materials

Minimal impact on:

  • Dielectrics (e.g. wood, plastic), where F0 is low

  • Smooth surfaces (low roughness)

Before vs After

Case | Before (Single Scatter) | After (Multi Scatter) -- | -- | -- Rough metals | Dark, dull | Brighter, richer Smooth metals | Similar | Similar Wood/plastic | No visible change | No visible change

Performance Impact

  • Negligible

  • Adds only a few arithmetic operations

  • No additional texture fetches

Notes

  • The implementation follows common real-time approximations used in modern renderers (e.g. Unreal Engine)

  • Care should be taken to avoid overcompensation; optional clamping can be added if needed

  • This change improves perceptual realism without altering the overall rendering pipeline

Testing

Tested with:

  • HDRI lighting environments

  • Roughness sweep (0.0 → 1.0)

  • Metallic materials (gold, steel, aluminum)

  • Dielectrics (wood, plastic)

Impact

This change:

  • Aligns Godot’s PBR model more closely with industry standards

  • Improves visual quality with minimal cost

  • Enhances material realism, especially in high-end rendering workflows

File Modified

  • shaders/scene_forward_clustered.glsl

If you want, I can also:

  • add a toggle flag (enable/disable multi-scatter)

  • match Unreal’s exact implementation more closely

  • or prepare comparison screenshots for the PR

## What this PR does

Initializes `msaa3d.color` in the internal buffer path when setting up 3D MSAA.

Without this, the setup check will treat the MSAA buffer as uninitialized and recreate it every frame. This causes unnecessary resource recreation and lead to leaks on android platform.

## Why

In the `use_internal_buffer` path, `msaa3d.fbo` is created, but `msaa3d.color` was not initialized before the setup state was checked again later.

Generating the renderbuffer here makes the MSAA state consistent with the rest of the setup flow and prevents repeated recreation.

- Built and ran the affected renderer path
- Verified the framebuffer setup still completes successfully
- Verified the MSAA 3D internal buffer is no longer recreated every frame

label.rationale: Names an LLM tool. Not labeled slop.

cases.body: ### Summary of changes Added the function `set_multicast_send_interface(if_name)` to `PacketPeerUDP` and `NetSocket`. This allows controlling the interface, through which a packet is sent to a multicast address. Before, the OS would choose an interface, so that the packet can reach it, but since it is a multicast address, it would choose a random one (so for example localhost or dummy0), which is useless, because the address can be reached using any interface. Internally, this sets `IPV6_MULTICAST_IF` and/or `IP_MULTICAST_IF` using `setsockopt(...)`. ### Example usage This allows sending packets to multicast addresses using all interfaces: ### Motivation This is an implementation of https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3109 Also, I myself have had the same problem with multicast, so I decided to fix it. Without this, functions like `join_mutlicast_group` in Godot are a bit (or a lot) useless, because the interface choices by the OS aren't consistent. ### Technical overview The user calls set_mutlicast_send_interface(interface_name) on the PacketPeerUDP, which will pass the argument to the underlaying NetSocket. Each platform group (Unix, Windows), then defines that function in its own way, but the main priciple is the same: If the socket ip_type covers IPv6, we find the interface index and call `setsockopt(_sock, IPPROTO_IPV6, IPV6_MULTICAST_IF, ...)` with it. If the socket ip_type covers IPv4, we find the first IPv4 address in the interface and call `setsockopt(_sock, IPPROTO_IP, IP_MULTICAST_IF, ...)` with it. ### Testing I have tested it, these connections worked first try (aside from firewall config): 1) Localhost (Almost any interface works locally) 2) Windows - WSL (Linux), using vEthernet (Hyper-V connection) 3) Windows - Windows, using Wi-Fi 4) Windows - Android, using Wi-Fi 5) Android - Android, using Wi-Fi 6) Windows - Ubuntu VM (VMWare Drivers) ### Discussion I am not sure if it works on iOS and MacOS, so testing with it could be good. ### AI Self Disclosure The `setsockopt(...)` lines were written by Claude. I made sure that the code makes sense, is readable and actually works, which means that I made changes to it. EDIT: I have read the documentation for setsockopt parameters, and made changes according to it. It's a bit cleaner and safer now, and I can say that all code in this is written by a human (everything that AI originally wrote isn't in the code).

cases.title: Fix: 1-tick lag when CharacterBody stands on a moving kinematic platform (2D + 3D)

label.rationale: Names an LLM tool. Not labeled slop.

cases.body:
## Summary of changes

New boolean property `platform_velocity_correction_beta` on `CharacterBody3D`/`CharacterBody2D`. When enabled, eliminates the one-physics-tick lag when a `CharacterBody3D` rides another `CharacterBody3D`.

### ⚠️ **Disclaimer:** This documentation was partially build by AI(claude). Also AI was involved into searching the codebase for the right place to put the fix. And help with initial understanding of a codebase around SceneTree and godot_physics_*. Some code comments was added by AI. But i Do have understanding of the code that i wrote and did test it with many scenarios


## Motivation

Bug report:
Fixes: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/101253

A `CharacterBody3D` standing on a `AnimatableBody3D` or `CharacterBody3D` that moving by `move_and_collide()` or `move_and_slide()`  always reads the platform's velocity from the **previous** tick, because `move_and_collide()` defers the physics body transform update via `xform_change_list`, which flushes only after all `_physics_process` callbacks complete. The lag scales visibly with speed.

## Technical overview

Three changes, applied identically to both 2D and 3D:

**1. Immediate physics body push** (`physics_body_3d.cpp`, `physics_body_2d.cpp`)
Before `set_global_transform()`, call `body_set_state(BODY_STATE_TRANSFORM)` directly on the physics server — bypassing `xform_change_list` so the new transform is available within the same tick.

**2. Pending velocity cache** (`modules/godot_physics_3d/`, `modules/godot_physics_2d/`)
When `body_set_state` fires for a kinematic body mid-step, compute and cache `pending_linear_velocity` / `pending_angular_velocity`. `GodotPhysicsDirectBodyState` getters return cached values while the flag is set. Flag clears at end of `GodotStep::step()`.

**3. Adaptive process ordering** (`scene_tree.cpp`, `node.h`, `CharacterBody3D/2D`)
`CharacterBody3D/2D` override `get_physics_process_dependency()` to return their floor node. `SceneTree::_process_group()` auto-swaps nodes with equal `physics_process_priority` so the platform always runs before the rider — no manual priority config needed, works for stacking chains of any depth.

## Testing

Tested on Windows 10, engine fork based on 4.6.2.

**Before fix** (stock 4.5/4.6):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/16ccee21-c594-40f0-90a5-a3f881690cda

**After fix:**

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/621bbf20-ec62-4f2c-8b26-ea4f448e33d3

Tested scenarios: `AnimatableBody3D` + `move_and_collide()`, `CharacterBody3D` + `move_and_slide()`, multi-level stacking, arbitrary scene tree order. different and same `physics_process_priority`

## Discussion

**Risks & caveats:**
- The auto-sort only works within a single process group (same `process_thread_group` + same priority). Cross-group cases still require manual `physics_process_priority`.
- If the rider has a *lower* `physics_process_priority` than the platform, auto-sort is intentionally skipped to respect explicit priority settings.
- `sync_to_physics = true` on `AnimatableBody` conflicts with `move_and_collide()` and should not be combined with this fix.
- Needs broader testing — stacking chains may interact with ceiling collisions in edge cases.
- This is my first engine contribution; I am not a professional C++ developer.

## Additional work & disclosure

I would appreciate feedback on the correctness of the `GodotStep` flag-clearing placement and the `SceneTree` swap logic.

Parts of this PR involved AI assistance (Claude): searching the codebase for the right integration points, understanding `SceneTree`/`godot_physics_*` internals, and some code comments. All logic was created, reviewed and tested by me personally.

cases.title: [iOS] Add AccessKit screen reader support

label.rationale: Names an LLM tool. Not labeled slop.

cases.body:
> [!NOTE]
> AI-assisted contribution disclosure:
Claude Code was used to help generate an initial boilerplate draft based on the existing macOS AccessKit implementation and to explore unfamiliar APIs. The generated code was not accepted as-is and required significant manual debugging, modification, integration work, and testing.
The implementation was built, exported, and tested manually on physical iOS hardware with VoiceOver enabled. Additional fixes and follow-up changes were made during review and integration.
This PR should be considered AI-assisted, not AI-authored.

## What problem(s) does this PR solve?

iOS is currently the only major Godot platform without screen reader support. macOS, Windows, and Linux already integrate the AccessKit-based `AccessibilityServerAccessKit` driver, but iOS has no implementation, so VoiceOver cannot read `Control` elements or their `accessibility_name` / `description` / `role` properties in apps exported from Godot.

This PR adds the missing iOS glue so VoiceOver works out of the box, using the same driver and the upstream `accesskit_ios_subclassing_adapter`.

- Closes #

## Additional information

### What changed

- **`drivers/accesskit/accessibility_server_accesskit.{h,cpp}`** - Adds an `APPLE_EMBEDDED_ENABLED` branch alongside the existing macOS / Windows / Linux paths in `window_create` / `window_destroy` / `update_if_active`, using AccessKit's 3-callback iOS variant.
- **`platform/apple_embedded/display_server_apple_embedded.{h,mm}`** - Registers `godotView` as the host `UIView` with `AccessibilityServer::window_create`, advertises `FEATURE_ACCESSIBILITY_SCREEN_READER`, and surfaces VoiceOver state via `accessibility_screen_reader_active()` backed by `UIAccessibilityIsVoiceOverRunning`.
- **`platform/ios/detect.py`** - Adds an `accesskit_sdk_path` SCons option mirroring the macOS pattern, links the appropriate device / simulator static slice, and defines `ACCESSKIT_ENABLED` when found.
- **`drivers/SCsub`** - Includes the AccessKit driver sources in the iOS build.

### Scope decisions

- **visionOS deliberately not enabled.** The `APPLE_EMBEDDED_ENABLED` guard would cover it, but visionOS is kept out of `drivers/SCsub` and `platform/visionos/detect.py` to limit this PR's scope. Happy to follow up in a separate PR.
- **No new script-exposed API.** No `doc/classes/` changes are required - the feature surfaces through the existing `AccessibilityServer` API and `Control.accessibility_*` properties already documented for the other platforms.

### Dependency status

This PR depends on **AccessKit C 0.22.1** (released 2026-05-24, [AccessKit/accesskit-c#94](https://github.com/AccessKit/accesskit-c/pull/94)), which introduces the iOS adapters.

A matching **godot-accesskit-c-static** release with iOS binaries (`lib/ios/{arm64,simulator_arm64}/static/libaccesskit.a`) is still pending. Until that lands, the PR can be built by compiling `accesskit-c` 0.22.1 locally and pointing `accesskit_sdk_path=...` at the resulting tree. **Suggest holding merge until the static-bindings release is cut.**

### Test plan

Manual VoiceOver testing - no automated tests added. The change is platform glue with no host-testable surface, matching how the macOS / Windows / Linux AccessKit integrations were merged.

Tested with VoiceOver enabled on:
- [x] iOS device (arm64) - `Control` nodes are reachable via swipe navigation; `accessibility_name`, `description`, and `role` are announced
- [x] Confirmed no regression with VoiceOver disabled

Reviewers wanting to reproduce: build `accesskit-c` 0.22.1 with the iOS targets, then:

```bash
scons platform=ios target=template_debug arch=arm64 accesskit_sdk_path=/path/to/accesskit-c
```

cases.title: Fix binary resource loading when the type hint is a script class

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
Fixes #90769.

### Root cause

`ResourceFormatLoaderBinary::get_recognized_extensions_for_type()` resolves extensions via `ClassDB::get_extensions_for_type()`. That only walks classes registered in `ClassDB`, but a script global class (`class_name` in GDScript) lives in `ScriptServer`'s global class list instead.

So when the requested type is a custom resource class, the lookup returns an empty list, `ResourceFormatLoader::recognize_path()` finds no matching extension and returns `false`, and the binary loader is skipped entirely. `ResourceLoader::_load()` then ends up with no loader at all and the load fails with:

```
ERROR: No loader found for resource: res://my_resource.res (expected type: MyResource)
```

`ResourceFormatLoaderText` is unaffected because it offers `tres` for any type that is not a `PackedScene` or `GDExtension`, without consulting `ClassDB`. That asymmetry is exactly why the type hint worked for `.tres` but not `.res`.

### Fix

When `ClassDB` yields no extensions and the type is a script global class, resolve the native class it ultimately extends via `ScriptServer::get_global_class_native_base()` and look up the extensions for that.

The new branch only runs in the case that was previously broken — when `ClassDB` already knows the type, the extension list is non-empty and behavior is unchanged.

### Testing

Added a regression test to `tests/core/io/test_resource.cpp`. It registers a script global class through `ScriptServer::add_global_class()`, saves the same resource as both `.tres` and `.res`, and asserts both load when the type hint names that class. It unregisters the class afterwards, and adds no fixture files to the repository.

Verified the test genuinely reproduces the bug. On `master` without the fix, the text assertion passes and the binary one fails:

```
tests\core\io\test_resource.cpp:593: ERROR: CHECK( loaded_binary.is_valid() ) is NOT correct!
  values: CHECK( false )
  logged: A binary resource should load when the type hint is a script global class.
[doctest] test cases: 1 | 0 passed | 1 failed
```

With the fix applied, the full suite passes:

```
[doctest] test cases:   1411 |   1411 passed | 0 failed | 3 skipped
[doctest] assertions: 421208 | 421208 passed | 0 failed |
```

Built with GCC 15.2 (MinGW/UCRT64) on Windows, `target=editor tests=yes`. Both changed files are clean under clang-format 22.1.5.

cases.title: GDScript: Allow integer index access on Quaternion

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
Fixes #120318.

### Root cause

In `GDScriptAnalyzer::reduce_subscript()`, `Variant::QUATERNION` was grouped with the types that accept a String index only (alongside `Rect2`, `Plane`, `AABB` and `Object`), so an integer index was rejected at parse time:

```
Invalid index type "int" for a base of type "Quaternion".
```

This contradicts the analyzer itself: a little further down, the same function already resolves the result of indexing a `Quaternion` to `float`, which only makes sense for integer indexing. `Quaternion` also provides `operator[](int)` in `core/math/quaternion.h`, and the documented `operator []` behaviour expects an int. Other types backed by the same kind of accessor — `Basis` and the `Vector` family — are already in the group that accepts a String *or* a number.

Thanks to @AThousandShips for pinpointing this in the issue thread.

### Fix

Move `Variant::QUATERNION` into the "Expect String or number" group. String indexing (`quaternion["z"]`) is unaffected, and no other type changes group.

### Testing

Added `modules/gdscript/tests/scripts/analyzer/features/quaternion_subscript.gd`, covering a constant integer index, a variable integer index, and a String index.

Verified it reproduces the bug. On `master` without the fix:

```
GDTEST_ANALYZER_ERROR
>> ERROR at line 6: Invalid index type "int" for a base of type "Quaternion".
>> ERROR at line 7: Invalid index type "int" for a base of type "Quaternion".
>> ERROR at line 11: Invalid index type "int" for a base of type "Quaternion".
```

Note the String index on the last line is not reported, matching the issue description. With the fix applied the full suite passes:

```
[doctest] test cases:   1411 |   1411 passed | 0 failed | 3 skipped
[doctest] assertions: 421209 | 421209 passed | 0 failed |
```

Built with GCC 15.2 (MinGW/UCRT64) on Windows, `target=editor tests=yes`. Clean under clang-format 22.1.5.

### Out of scope

The issue thread also notes that `Transform3D` sits in the opposite wrong group — it accepts an integer index in the analyzer but has no subscript operator, so it fails at runtime rather than at parse time. That is a separate behavioural change and is deliberately left out of this PR.

## What problem(s) does this PR solve?

Gives uniformity to our core logic that relies on narrowing templates to their basic types by wholly replacing `GetSimpleTypeT` (an alias for `std::remove_cv_t<std::remove_reference_t<T>>`) with the far more appropriate and less verbose `std::decay_t`.

And it claimed to have found the bug, patched the bug, documented the bug. The reason that this appeared in the Mali GPU variant but not the Windows/NVIDIA variant was explained to me the following way: The Godot 3.6 GLES3 render can run in mobile or desktop mode and in mobile mode the lighting is calculated per vertex instead of per fragment. The bug sits in this conditional vertex exeution path. It had nothing to do with my TV specifically and should also be relevant for most android exports. The follwing description is written by luna again, after me grilling it, doubting it and asking to explain it to me. The fix is about ten AI-written lines of code and I read them five times at least. I am now 85% sure that this is correct, mind you that I am not a shader expert, but at least I did write some tiny WebGL1 shaders as coursework seven years ago. Note that this is tested as just desribed. There is also a fix included for the toon shader branch, which is untested. > ### Problem > > In Godot 3’s GLES3 renderer, materials using USE_VERTEX_LIGHTING calculate direct light contributions in the vertex shader. The resulting direct specular lighting is passed to the fragment shader through specular_light_interp. > > The fragment shader then adds image-based lighting to the same specular_light accumulator: > > ```text > specular_light = > direct vertex-computed specular > + environment/reflection-probe specular > ``` > > Directional shadowing is applied afterwards. The shader used specular_light_interp.a to determine how strongly the directional shadow should affect the interpolated direct lighting: > > ```glsl > specular_light *= mix(vec3(1.0), > light_attenuation, > specular_light_interp.a); > ``` > > specular_light_interp.a is a pre-shadow weighting value. It represents the fraction of the direct vertex-computed specular lighting attributable to the directional light. It is not a measure of the fragment’s total lighting and does not indicate whether the fragment is currently lit or shadowed. > > With one dominant DirectionalLight, this value is normally close to 1.0. If the shadow map then determines that the fragment is fully shadowed, light_attenuation is approximately zero and the expression becomes: > > ```text > (direct specular + indirect specular) × 0 > ``` > > The direct directional highlight is correctly removed, but the environment and reflection-probe specular is removed incorrectly as well. > > The intended result is: > > ```text > (direct specular × shadow factor) + indirect specular > ``` > > This can make metallic materials lose their environment reflections in shadows and become unnaturally flat or dark. The remaining constant ambient lighting may still keep them visible, so the result does not necessarily become black. > > The fragment-lighting path does not have this accumulation problem. It retains indirect specular in the accumulator and passes shadow attenuation directly to light_compute(), which applies it only while calculating the direct light contribution. > > ### Fix > > The vertex-lighting path now tracks direct and indirect specular lighting separately. > > A new vertex_specular_light variable stores the direct specular value received from the vertex shader: > > ```glsl > vec3 vertex_specular_light = specular_light_interp.rgb; > specular_light = vertex_specular_light; > ``` > > Environment and reflection-probe lighting continues to be accumulated into specular_light. > > After the existing material/BRDF scaling, the indirect component is derived: > > ```glsl > vec3 indirect_specular_light = > specular_light - vertex_specular_light; > ``` > > Directional shadow attenuation is applied only to vertex_specular_light: > > ```glsl > vertex_specular_light *= mix(vec3(1.0), > light_attenuation, > specular_light_interp.a); > ``` > > The two components are then recombined: > > ```glsl > specular_light = > indirect_specular_light + vertex_specular_light; > ``` > > The toon and regular BRDF branches both scale vertex_specular_light with the same specular_scale used for specular_light, preserving the existing unshadowed material behavior. > > ### Shader variants and performance > > The new variables and calculations are guarded by USE_VERTEX_LIGHTING. The fragment-lighting variant remains unchanged. > > The patch does not move direct lighting into the fragment shader. Direct light calculations remain vertex-based, with no new per-pixel light loops, texture samples, varyings, or shadow-map lookups. > > The vertex-lighting fragment variant performs a small amount of additional vector bookkeeping: separate scaling, subtraction, and recombination. This may slightly increase register pressure, but preserves the intended performance advantage of vertex lighting. So without AI nothing of this would have been possible. cases.title: TileSetAtlasSource.create_tile() is O(n²) - large tilesets take tens of seconds to load

label.rationale: Slop, hallucination, or AI-generated language in the text. Not a patch-marker fail.

cases.body:
### Tested versions

- Reproducible in 4.7.2.stable.official.ed1daf0bf
- Present in source from at least 4.4-stable through 4.7-stable

### System information

Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS - Intel Core i9-14900KF (32 threads), 62 GB RAM - Godot 4.7.2.stable, GL Compatibility, headless

### Issue description

**Human Foreword:** I had this issue dealing with a large tileset and had claude diagnose, find the fix then generate this ticket. Hope that doesn't count as AI slop-pyness but it is an actual issue was lagging the hell out of my game and the fix worked. I checked that it hadn't already been reported and it still exists in the current build.

Loading a large 16x16 tileset of about 56k tiles took about 43 seconds when running the game and brought the editor to a crawl, after trying different things it wasn't directly that there was a lot of tiles that was the problem, it was due to the godot code resorting every time a tile was initialized and added, splitting the same 56k tiles into separate sheets and then including all of them in the exact same board reduced load to about 1.3s. Problem isn't the large tile count, it's the way they're built internally.

Clanker probably wrote it up better below.

---

`TileSetAtlasSource::create_tile()` re-sorts the entire `tiles_ids` vector on every single insertion
(`scene/resources/2d/tile_set.cpp`, in 4.7-stable at line 5014):

```cpp
// Create and resize the tile.
tiles.insert(p_atlas_coords, tad);
tiles_ids.push_back(p_atlas_coords);
tiles_ids.sort();          // full re-sort, once per tile

_create_coords_mapping_cache(p_atlas_coords);
_queue_update_padded_texture();
```

with `Vector<Vector2i> tiles_ids;` declared in `scene/resources/2d/tile_set.h`.

Building a source of `n` tiles therefore costs `Σ k·log k ≈ (n²/2)·log₂ n` comparisons rather than a
single `O(n log n)` sort at the end. `remove_tile()` (line 5036) and `move_tile_in_atlas()` (line 5387)
re-sort the same way.

This is reached once per tile during resource loading. `TileSetAtlasSource::_set()` handles each
`"<x>:<y>/0"` property with:

```cpp
if (!has_tile(coords)) {
    create_tile(coords);
}
```

so a `.tres` defining `n` tiles pays the full quadratic cost on load.

The practical effect is that a tileset built from a large commercial atlas — the kind that ships as one
sheet of tens of thousands of 16×16 tiles — takes tens of seconds to load, and the same cost is paid
again on every edit in the TileSet editor. It is not obvious to users that tile *count* is the cause:
the natural suspects (texture size, VRAM, `use_texture_padding`, text vs. binary serialisation) are all
measurably irrelevant by comparison.

## Suggested fix

Sort lazily rather than eagerly. Replace the `tiles_ids.sort()` calls in `create_tile()`,
`remove_tile()` and `move_tile_in_atlas()` with a dirty flag, and sort on first read in the accessors
that depend on the ordering (`get_tile_id()`, and iteration over `tiles_ids`). That reduces bulk
construction from `O(n² log n)` to `O(n log n)` while leaving observable ordering unchanged.

A smaller change — `tiles_ids.ordered_insert()` in place of `push_back()` + `sort()` — keeps the vector
sorted at all times and cuts the constant factor substantially, but remains `O(n²)` because of the
element shifting.

## Workaround for users

Split the atlas across multiple `TileSetAtlasSource` entries, or multiple smaller tilesets. Per the
table above this gives close to an N× speedup for N sources, with no reduction in the number of tiles
available. Many commercial packs that ship a single merged sheet also ship the same art pre-split by
category; importing those instead is the least invasive route.


### Steps to reproduce

Self-contained, no external assets. Run with
`godot --headless --path <project> --script res://repro.gd`:

```gdscript
extends SceneTree


## Times TileSetAtlasSource.create_tile() as the tile count grows
func _initialize() -> void:
	for tile_target: int in [1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000]:
		# Build an empty atlas source over a placeholder texture
		var texture := PlaceholderTexture2D.new()
		texture.size = Vector2(2816, 8224)
		var source := TileSetAtlasSource.new()
		source.texture = texture
		source.texture_region_size = Vector2i(16, 16)
		source.use_texture_padding = false

		# Create tiles one at a time, as the resource loader does
		var started_usec: int = Time.get_ticks_usec()
		var created: int = 0
		for y: int in 514:
			for x: int in 176:
				source.create_tile(Vector2i(x, y))
				created += 1
				if created >= tile_target:
					break
			if created >= tile_target:
				break
		var elapsed_usec: int = Time.get_ticks_usec() - started_usec

		print("%6d tiles: %8.3f s" % [created, elapsed_usec / 1000000.0])
	quit()
```

Observed:

| Tiles | Time | × previous |
|------:|------:|-----------:|
| 1,000 | 0.008 s | — |
| 2,000 | 0.036 s | 4.50 |
| 4,000 | 0.164 s | 4.55 |
| 8,000 | 0.714 s | 4.35 |
| 16,000 | 3.020 s | 4.23 |
| 32,000 | 12.632 s | 4.18 |

Each doubling of tile count roughly quadruples the time, as expected for `O(n²)`.

### Confirmation against a real tileset

A `TileSet` over a 2816×8224 atlas at 16×16, `use_texture_padding = false`, texture pre-warmed and
excluded from the measurement, loaded with `CACHE_MODE_IGNORE` in a fresh process (median of 3, or mean
of 2 above 16,000):

| Tiles | Load |
|------:|------:|
| 1,000 | 0.09 s |
| 4,000 | 0.27 s |
| 16,000 | 3.19 s |
| 32,000 | 13.19 s |
| 56,639 | **41.51 s** |

Fitting `t ≈ 1.228×10⁻⁵ n²` ms on the mid-range points predicts 12.6 s and 39.4 s for the last two rows
against measured 13.2 s and 41.5 s — within 5%.

Comparing the two tables at 32,000 tiles (12.63 s via the API, 13.19 s via a `.tres`) puts text parsing
at roughly 4% of load time. Serialising to binary `.res` does not measurably help, and neither does
`use_texture_padding = false`; both are dominated by this.

### The cost is per source, not per tileset

Splitting the identical 56,639 tiles across more `TileSetAtlasSource` entries in a single `TileSet`
over the same texture — every file below contains all 56,639 tiles, verified by summing
`get_tiles_count()` across sources:

| Sources | Tiles each | Load | Speedup |
|--------:|-----------:|------:|--------:|
| 1 | 56,639 | 41.51 s | — |
| 2 | 28,320 | 20.41 s | 2.03× |
| 4 | 14,160 | 10.03 s | 4.14× |
| 8 | 7,080 | 4.99 s | 8.32× |
| 16 | 3,540 | 2.54 s | 16.33× |
| 32 | 1,770 | 1.34 s | 31.06× |

The speedup is linear in the number of sources, consistent with `n²` cost accumulating independently
within each source's own `tiles_ids`.

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

N/A - Single script in steps to reproduce above

Prior research made for this patch was AI-driven as well as some parts of this code. Although I understand the changes AI made and tried cleaning the code from AI slop, I've used it to speed up writing the patch as well
## What problem(s) does this PR solve?

With many draw calls, the Forward+ render list repeats two lookups for every element:

- `add_draw_list_bind_vertex_buffers()` calls `buffer_get_dynamic_offsets()`, which reads every buffer's driver info, although mesh vertex arrays never hold dynamic persistent buffers (the mask is always 0).
- `_render_list_template()` calls `mesh_surface_get_vertex_arrays_and_format()`, which takes the surface's version_lock, even when the previous element in the sorted list drew the same surface with the same inputs.

In a scene with about 9 000 draw calls (Vulkan, separate rendering thread), these took about 13% of the rendering thread.

This PR records in VertexArray whether it has a dynamic buffer and skips the lookup if not. It also reuses the previous element's vertex array when the surface and its inputs are unchanged. The commands sent to the GPU are identical. The frame rate change in my test stayed within noise (paused scene, same build flags: 105.4–108.9 FPS before, 106.9–107.7 after), so the benefit is lower CPU time per draw on the rendering thread.

## Additional information

This was spotted while I was working on a train sim. Here are some benchmark results from the most "demanding" scenery with the mentioned 9 000 draw calls (Vulkan, separate rendering thread):
4.7.2.stable without a patch: ~8.76 ms per frame
4.7.2.stable with a patch ~8.45 ms per frame

cases.title: GLES3: Fix index buffer target in mesh_surface_update_index_region

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
## What problem(s) does this PR solve?

Closes [Trail3D (and mesh_surface_update_index_region) produce no geometry on Web: index buffer is bound to GL_ARRAY_BUFFER #124726](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/124726)

In `MeshStorage::mesh_surface_update_index_region()`, the index buffer was being bound to `GL_ARRAY_BUFFER` instead of `GL_ELEMENT_ARRAY_BUFFER`.

While desktop OpenGL drivers silently tolerate target mismatches for `glBufferSubData()`, OpenGL ES 3.0 and WebGL 2.0 strictly disallow binding a buffer allocated as `GL_ELEMENT_ARRAY_BUFFER` to a different target:
`WebGL: INVALID_OPERATION: bindBuffer: element array buffers can not be bound to a different target`

This caused dynamic index updates (such as those done each frame by `Trail3D` or procedural mesh updates) to fail on Web exports, causing the mesh to render no geometry.

## Additional information

The fix corrects the binding target in `mesh_surface_update_index_region()` to `GL_ELEMENT_ARRAY_BUFFER`.

In OpenGL ES / WebGL, the element array buffer binding is stored as part of the Vertex Array Object (VAO) state rather than global context state. We unbind the active VAO (`glBindVertexArray(0)`) before binding `GL_ELEMENT_ARRAY_BUFFER` so that unbinding the buffer at the end does not clear the element buffer of whatever VAO is currently active.

Additionally:
- Added a check to ensure `mesh->surfaces[p_surface]->index_buffer != 0` before updating to guard non-indexed surfaces safely.
- In `mesh_add_surface()`, marked `index_buffer` with `GL_DYNAMIC_DRAW` when `ARRAY_FLAG_USE_DYNAMIC_UPDATE` is specified (previously hardcoded to `GL_STATIC_DRAW`), matching how vertex, attribute, and skin buffers are handled.

## AI disclosure

AI was used to help research the WebGL specification constraints and analyze the VAO state binding behavior. I implemented the fix and verified the changes and formatting against the codebase.

cases.title: tinyexr: Bound uncompressed HALF->HALF scanline copy against data_len

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
## Summary

In `thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.h`, `tinyexr::DecodePixelData()` (`lines 5591-5710`) decodes uncompressed scanline pixel data (`compression_type == TINYEXR_COMPRESSIONTYPE_NONE`) across four pixel-type sub-branches. Three of the four sub-branches verify that reading `width` elements from `line_ptr` does not exceed `data_ptr + data_len`:

- **`HALF -> FLOAT`** (`thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.h:5629-5633`):
  ```cpp
  if (reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char *>(line_ptr + width) >
      (data_ptr + data_len)) {
    // Insufficient data size
    return false;
  }
  ```
- **`FLOAT -> FLOAT`** (`thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.h:5664-5668`): checks `reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char *>(line_ptr + width) > (data_ptr + data_len)`.
- **`UINT -> UINT`** (`thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.h:5692-5696`): checks `reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char *>(line_ptr + width) > (data_ptr + data_len)`.

However, the first sub-branch — **`HALF -> HALF`** (`channels[c].pixel_type == TINYEXR_PIXELTYPE_HALF && requested_pixel_types[c] == TINYEXR_PIXELTYPE_HALF`, `thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.h:5600-5619`) — omits this check and immediately loops `for (int u = 0; u < width; u++)` calling `tinyexr::cpy2(&(hf.u), line_ptr + u)` (`line 5614`). Because `DecodeChunk` only checks that a scanline chunk's declared `data_len` fits within the remaining input buffer without requiring `data_len >= width * pixel_data_size`, a truncated or malformed uncompressed `HALF` scanline chunk with `data_len < width * sizeof(uint16_t)` causes `LoadEXRImageFromMemory` / `LoadEXRImageFromFile` (which default `requested_pixel_types[c]` to `TINYEXR_PIXELTYPE_HALF`) to read past `data_ptr + data_len` (heap-based buffer over-read, `CWE-125`).

## Impact on Godot

- Similar to `GH-124638` (`3e7eda1f0838c0ac5ce6eac023dbb0df8c40d10b`), Godot's `ImageLoaderTinyEXR::load_image` (`modules/tinyexr/image_loader_tinyexr.cpp:74-80`, `GH-13490`) sets `exr_header.requested_pixel_types[i] = TINYEXR_PIXELTYPE_FLOAT` for `TINYEXR_PIXELTYPE_HALF` channels (taking the guarded `HALF -> FLOAT` branch at line `5629` before converting back to `FORMAT_RH`/`RGH`/`RGBH`/`RGBAH` via `Math::make_half_float`), while `thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.cc` compiles the full `TINYEXR_IMPLEMENTATION` (`LoadEXRImageFromMemory` / `LoadEXRImageFromFile`) with the unguarded `HALF -> HALF` loop in `DecodePixelData`.
- This PR adds the matching `reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char *>(line_ptr + width) > (data_ptr + data_len)` guard to the `HALF -> HALF` sub-branch (`thirdparty/tinyexr/tinyexr.h:5610`). (If desired, we can also add a corresponding `thirdparty/tinyexr/patches/0003-fix-uncompressed-half-scanline-bounds.patch` file and `thirdparty/README.md` entry referencing this PR number.)

## Testing

- Verified with `SaveEXRImageToMemory` -> `LoadEXRImageFromMemory` native-`HALF` (`TINYEXR_COMPRESSIONTYPE_NONE`) round-trips and truncated-chunk inputs under both Release (`-O3 -DNDEBUG`) and AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address,undefined`).

---
*Note: This patch was prepared with AI assistance and verified by human review and local test execution.*

cases.title: macOS: Fix universal export using the wrong template build

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
## What problem(s) does this PR solve?

- Closes #124744

Universal macOS exports inverted which template binaries they kept. `--export-release` packaged the debug `.arm64` and `.x86_64` slices, and `--export-debug` packaged the release slices. Single-architecture exports were unaffected.

`EditorExportPlatformMacOS::export_project` skips template entries that are not the selected build. The universal branch introduced in #124408 skipped files that *did* match `binary_to_use_base` (`godot_macos_release.` or `godot_macos_debug.`). This negates that test so both architecture slices of the requested build are kept and the other build is skipped, matching the non-universal branch.

## Additional information

Use of AI: an autonomous coding assistant (Cursor, Grok) located the inverted `begins_with` check from issue #124744, applied the one-line condition change, and opened this pull request on behalf of Bit-Byte5. The diagnosis and the proposed negation come from the issue report; the change was not otherwise verified by running a macOS export locally.
